title: Universal childcare can have long-run maternal work and fiscal effects beyond preschool years
source_unit: NBER Working Paper 35514; Quebec universal subsidized childcare program and long-run maternal labor, earnings, benefit, and tax outcomes
geography: Quebec, Canada; comparative policy evidence for U.S. childcare and work-capacity analysis

observations.period: Quebec universal subsidized childcare program; working paper issued July 2026

denominator.unit: mothers exposed to Quebec childcare-policy variation; exact analytic denominator is source-specific

long_run_employment.unit: maternal employment effect after children aged out of preschool

long_run_earnings.value: positive and growing to about twice the participation effect
long_run_earnings.unit: long-run maternal earnings effect relative to employment effect

occupational_upgrading.unit: reported occupational and within-occupation career changes

fiscal_recapture.unit: percent of upfront costs potentially recaptured by the estimated net present value of fiscal benefits

observations.method: Longitudinal policy evaluation of Quebec's universal subsidized childcare program, estimating effects on maternal labor supply, earnings, social-program benefit receipt, tax remittances, occupational movement, and fiscal balance.
observations.uncertainty: This is comparative Canadian evidence, not a U.S. treatment estimate. The abstract does not disclose the full analytic denominator or all implementation details. Long-run employment and earnings do not establish equal slot access, care quality, child outcomes, maternal wellbeing, schedule control, or transferability to U.S. institutions and labor markets. Fiscal recapture is a model-based estimate.
observations.subgroup: Mothers exposed to Quebec's universal subsidized childcare policy and lifecycle outcomes after preschool; the design and institutional setting differ from U.S. childcare programs and should remain separate.
observations.counterinterpretation: Effects may depend on Quebec's prices, labor-market institutions, parental leave, provider system, tax-benefit rules, and broader policy package. Increased employment can coexist with care burden, quality variation, unequal use, or reduced time in other activities.

boundary: This comparative record adds a long-run childcare-to-career-and-fiscal-persistence mechanism. It does not establish a U.S. policy effect, universal access, care quality, child wellbeing, maternal time satisfaction, or a causal cultural or political response.
